title: The cheap road that never got built
hook: Build the cheapest roads first. Does every cheap road make the cut?

knows: a spanning tree joins all towns with no loops (connect-the-towns-cheaply)
union-find tells whether two towns are already in the same group
doesNotKnow: that sorting all the roads first and skipping the ones that close a loop also finds the cheapest tree

misconception: The cheapest road is always built, and the roads skipped are the expensive ones.
objective: The learner can explain that Kruskal's method tests roads cheapest first and skips a road exactly when its towns are already connected, so on this map the 4-cost road A-B is skipped while the 5-cost road B-D is built, and the result is 4 roads (one fewer than towns) with total 11.

claims.text: Testing A-C 1, B-C 2, D-E 3, A-B 4, B-D 5, A-D 7, C-D 8, C-E 10 cheapest first builds A-C, B-C, D-E and B-D and skips the other four: 4 roads, total cost 11.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run(), a union-find replay the stage itself uses; builder re-ran it in a separate node script (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs), 2026-10-14: built AC, BC, DE, BD, total 11. Matches brief cs.algorithms #50. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own union-find replay (fc21/mst.mjs): build AC, BC, DE; skip AB; build BD; skip AD, CD, CE; total 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 11.

claims.text: A-B (cost 4) is skipped although it is cheaper than B-D (cost 5), because A and B are already joined through C.
claims.source: Same replay: after A-C and B-C, find(A) = find(B). Demo.tsx run(). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Same replay: after AC and BC, A and B share a root; AB (4) skipped, BD (5) built. Reveal reads CHEAPEST_SKIP and ROADS[4].

claims.text: A road is skipped only when its towns are already connected; building it would close a loop.
claims.source: If u and v are already connected, a path u..v exists among built roads, and adding u-v closes a cycle with it; otherwise no such path exists and the road joins two groups. CLRS 4e section 21.2 (MST-KRUSKAL tests FIND-SET(u) != FIND-SET(v)). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Cycle argument as given; Demo.tsx run() skips exactly when find(a) === find(b). CLRS 4e 21.2 recalled, not opened; derivation is self-contained.

claims.text: Kruskal's method ends with one road fewer than towns, and no tree joining all five towns costs less than 11.
claims.source: Any spanning tree on n vertices has n - 1 edges (CLRS 4e appendix B.5.1). Kruskal returns a minimum spanning tree by the cut property (CLRS 4e section 21.1, Corollary 21.2; 21.2). Builder also enumerated all spanning trees of this 8-road map in node (scratchpad algo2b0/check2.mjs): minimum total 11, achieved only by AC, BC, DE, BD. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Own enumeration of all 4-edge subsets: 40 spanning trees, minimum 11, unique (AC, BC, DE, BD); n - 1 = 4 roads. CLRS section numbers recalled, not opened; the claim rests on the enumeration.

claims.text: Towns in the same colour are already connected by built roads.
claims.source: Stage convention: each town is coloured by its union-find representative (alphabetically first town in its group). Demo.tsx COLOUR / run(). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: Demo.tsx fills each town with COLOUR[group[t]]; union keeps the alphabetically smaller root, so the root is the group's first town. Stage note 'Same colour = already connected.'

recall.question: Building roads cheapest first, you reach a cost-2 road whose two towns are already connected through other built roads. What happens to it?
options: It is skipped, because it would close a loop
It is built, because it is cheap
It replaces the most expensive road built so far
recall.why: Kruskal skips a road exactly when its towns are already in the same group, however cheap it is: building it would only add a loop.

references.note: Kruskal's algorithm with a disjoint-set forest
